mcqs.q: An extra-oral radiograph is especially useful when:
opts: Intra-oral views are impossible (gagging, trismus, unconscious) or a large region is needed
Only a single tooth crown must be seen
mcqs.explain: Extra-oral films (cassette outside the mouth) are used for large regions and when the patient cannot tolerate intra-oral films (gagging, trismus, unconscious).

mcqs.q: For the oblique mandibular BODY view, the central beam is aimed at the molar-premolar region:
opts: 2 cm below the angle of the OPPOSITE side of the mandible
mcqs.explain: The cassette is held against the side of interest and the beam is aimed at the molar-premolar region 2 cm below the opposite-side angle of the mandible.

mcqs.q: For a lateral skull radiograph, the image receptor is positioned:
opts: Parallel to the mid-sagittal plane, with the ray centred over the external auditory meatus
Perpendicular to the mid-sagittal plane, centred on the chin
mcqs.explain: The receptor is parallel to the mid-sagittal plane; the central ray is perpendicular to it and centred over the external auditory meatus.

mcqs.q: Which lesion is best investigated on a LATERAL skull view?
opts: Pituitary tumour expanding the sella turcica
mcqs.explain: The lateral skull shows the sella turcica (pituitary tumours), skull vault (Paget's, myeloma, hyperparathyroidism) and is used for cephalometry.

mcqs.q: In the submento-vertex (SMV) view, the patient's head is positioned so that:
opts: It is tipped back until the vertex touches the film, with the beam from below the chin
The forehead and nose touch the film
The nose and chin touch the film at 37°
It faces the film with the beam horizontal
mcqs.explain: For the SMV the head is tipped back so the vertex touches the film; the tube is aimed up from below the chin at ~5° to horizontal.

mcqs.q: The SMV view, with reduced exposure factors, is the classic projection for:
mcqs.explain: The SMV (with reduced exposure) shows the thin zygomatic arches; it also images the skull base, sphenoid sinus and posterior-mandible thickness before osteotomy.

mcqs.q: The Water's (occipitomental) projection is taken with the head in the:
opts: "Nose-chin" position, canthomeatal line at 37° to the receptor
Head tipped back, vertex on film
Mid-sagittal plane parallel to the film
mcqs.explain: Water's is an occipitomental 37° view in the nose-chin position, with the beam centred on the maxillary sinuses.

mcqs.q: The Water's projection is BEST for:
opts: The maxillary (paranasal) sinuses and middle-third facial fractures
mcqs.explain: Water's shows the maxillary sinuses and middle-third facial fractures (Le Fort, coronoid process).

mcqs.q: For a postero-anterior (PA) skull view, the patient is in the:
opts: "Forehead-nose" position with the central ray horizontal (0°) through the occiput
Head tipped back, beam from below the chin
Mid-sagittal plane parallel to the film
mcqs.explain: The PA skull is taken facing the film (forehead-nose) with a horizontal (0°) central ray centred through the occiput.

mcqs.q: The PA skull view is used to investigate:
opts: Skull-vault fractures and the frontal sinuses
mcqs.explain: The PA skull shows vault fractures, frontal sinuses and cranial conditions (Paget's, myeloma, hyperparathyroidism, intracranial calcification).

mcqs.q: In the reverse-Towne (open-mouth) projection, the mouth is opened in order to:
opts: Move the condylar heads out of the glenoid fossae so they can be seen
mcqs.explain: Opening the mouth drops the condyles out of the glenoid fossae, making the condylar heads visible on the reverse-Towne view.

mcqs.q: The reverse-Towne view is indicated for:
opts: High condylar-neck and intracapsular TMJ fractures
mcqs.explain: Reverse-Towne shows high condylar-neck fractures, intracapsular TMJ fractures and condylar hypo-/hyperplasia.

mcqs.q: In the reverse-Towne view, the central ray is directed:
opts: 30° upward from below the occiput, through the condyles
mcqs.explain: The tube is aimed upward from below the occiput with the central ray at 30° to horizontal, centred through the condyles.

mcqs.q: Which projection would you choose to assess a suspected ZYGOMATIC ARCH fracture?
mcqs.explain: The SMV (with reduced exposure) best demonstrates the thin zygomatic arches.

mcqs.q: Which projection best shows the MAXILLARY SINUSES?
mcqs.explain: Water's projection is the classic view of the maxillary (and paranasal) sinuses.

mcqs.q: Skull-vault conditions such as Paget's disease, multiple myeloma and hyperparathyroidism are typically evaluated on:
mcqs.explain: Lateral and PA skull projections demonstrate the cranial vault, where Paget's disease, multiple myeloma and hyperparathyroidism produce changes.

mcqs.q: Which projection requires the head tipped fully BACK with the beam aimed from below the chin?
mcqs.explain: Only the SMV tips the head back so the vertex touches the film, with the beam from below the chin.

mcqs.q: The reverse-Towne and lateral skull views are both relevant to the TMJ, but the reverse-Towne is preferred when you need to see the:
opts: Condylar heads free of the fossae (open mouth)
mcqs.explain: Reverse-Towne (open mouth) projects the condylar heads clear of the glenoid fossae, ideal for condylar fractures and morphology.

mcqs.q: The oblique mandibular RAMUS view centres the beam on the ramus, taken from:
opts: 2 cm below the inferior border of the opposite side of the mandible
mcqs.explain: For the ramus view the central beam is directed toward the centre of the imaged ramus from 2 cm below the opposite-side inferior border.

mcqs.q: Which view uses the canthomeatal line set at 37° to the image receptor?
mcqs.explain: Water's (occipitomental 37°) positions the canthomeatal line at 37° to the receptor in the nose-chin position.

mcqs.q: A generic indication shared by most extra-oral skull projections is:
opts: Assessment of maxillofacial fractures, cysts/tumours and TMJ disorders
Measuring crestal bone in localized periodontitis
mcqs.explain: Extra-oral projections assess maxillofacial/skull fractures, antra, TMJ disorders, cysts/tumours, osteomyelitis and growth — not fine intra-oral detail like caries.

mcqs.q: Which projection is taken with the patient FACING the film and a HORIZONTAL beam?
mcqs.explain: The PA skull is taken facing the film (forehead-nose) with a horizontal (0°) central ray; reverse-Towne also faces the film but angles the beam 30° upward.

saqs.q: List four general indications for extra-oral radiography.
saqs.a: Maxillofacial/skull fractures, cysts/tumours, TMJ disorders, sinus/antral disease, osteomyelitis, growth & development, and when intra-oral films are impossible (gagging, trismus, unconscious).

saqs.q: Describe the positioning and central ray for a lateral skull view.
saqs.a: Receptor parallel to the mid-sagittal plane; central ray perpendicular to the MSP, centred over the external auditory meatus.

saqs.q: How is the SMV positioned and what is it used for?
saqs.a: Head tipped back, vertex touches the film; beam from below the chin at 5°. Shows the skull base, sphenoid sinus, zygomatic arches and posterior-mandible thickness before osteotomy.

saqs.q: Give the position, key angle and main use of Water's projection.
saqs.a: Nose-chin position, canthomeatal line at 37° (occipitomental). Main use: maxillary/paranasal sinuses and middle-third facial fractures (Le Fort).

saqs.q: Contrast the PA skull and reverse-Towne positioning.
saqs.a: Both face the film (forehead-nose). PA: ray horizontal (0°) through occiput — vault/frontal sinus. Reverse-Towne: ray 30° upward, open mouth — condyles/TMJ.

saqs.q: Which projection best demonstrates the mandibular condyles, and why open the mouth?
saqs.a: Reverse-Towne; opening the mouth moves the condylar heads out of the glenoid fossae so they can be seen clear of overlapping bone.

saqs.q: Match each: zygomatic arches, maxillary sinus, condylar fracture, sella turcica — to a projection.
saqs.a: Zygomatic arches → SMV; maxillary sinus → Water's; condylar fracture → reverse-Towne; sella turcica → lateral skull.
